full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in SA No. 402 of 1975. 

 2. Plaintiff-respondent instituted Title Suit No. 106 of 1966 in theist Court of Subordinate Judge. Mymensingh, against the defendant-appellants praying for declaration of title to the land in suit appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 95 of Mouza Mymensingh town bearing Municipal holding No. 231 (present holding No. 66 and 66A) and for recovery of khas possession after demolishing the structures standing thereon. 

 5. The trial court upon consideration of the evidence and facts and circumstances of the case dismissed the suit holding that the Municipality was a lessee under the Maharaja by a patty which could not be substantiated by the production of it and in this context it was held. ; '"The Municipality was only the trustee of the Maharaja with regard to the land in suit". Next it was found that the defendants raised some pucca structures in violation of the terms of the lease "their possession as adverse to the knowledge of the Municipality which as such both of them acquired tenancy right by adverse possession". Lastly, it was found "that after the wholesale acquisition the Government has recognised the defendant as tenant." In this view of the matter, the suit was dismissed. 

 Plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 403 of 1963 and the learned Additional District Judge after bearing the parties concurred with the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. 

 6. Plaintiff filed second appeal being Second. Appeal No. 402 of 1975.  The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division allowed the appeal and decreed the plaintiff's suit in part after setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below. The High Court Division found that the defendants did not acquire tenancy right in the suit land under the Government. 

 Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel, appearing for the defendant-appellants, contended that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that upon the wholesale acquisition of the rent receiving. interest by the Government the defendants  did not acquire any tenancy right. The learned Counsel argued that since the land originally, belonged to Maharaja, a rent receiver, after the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest Government became the owner of it, and consequently by operation of law the defendants became tenants of the Government and as such the suit is not maintainable. 

 9. The Bengal Municipal Act 1932 provided the constitution of the Municipally and it provided further that the Municipality is a legal person which could sue and be sued. See section 15(2). It could also own land and dispose of it. See sections 91 & 95 of the Bengal Municipal Act 1932. It. can acquire and dispose of property. It can acquire land within or outside municipality compulsorily through the Government. See section 98(1). It is unfortunate that the appellate court found the entrustment" of the and of Maharaja to the Municipality which neither as a fact was proved nor could it be so because by operation of law land vested in the Municipality and it became owner. 

 13. It is undeniable fact that the land vested in the Municipality since 1932 and therefore, the defendant were only tenants of the land belonging to the Municipality by taking a temporary lease for nine years which however was renewed from time to time. The teamed Courts below unfortunately did not approach the facts of the case from the correct legal aspect. The High Court Division repelled the contention that after the wholesale acquisition by the Government the defendant has become a tenant under the Government and that the Maharaja has lost his paramount interest. This contention was repelled by the High Court Division by saying "the plaintiff is very much the owner of the suit land and cannot be denied any relief in the suit on the ground that it has lost its title," Mr. Pal argued that the question was not answered in the judgments of the courts below as to how this suit land vested in the Municipality and how it is exonerated from the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The answer is what we have given already that by the general notification affecting the rent receiving interest and the khas land of the rent receiver, the land which has vested with the Municipality since 1932 was not affected and therefore, the contentious of the defendants do not hold good, And. secondly the defendants' plea of adverse possession, as noticed already, has no substance. The trial court found that the defendants had constructed pucca structures in violation of the terms of the kabuliyat and these structures were raised some 20/25 years back. The view was taken that their possession "was adverse to the knowledge of Municipality' and in these circumstances "the Municipality was with the right of collecting cent and tax only as in the meantime the defendant 1 and his brother acquired tenancy right by adverse possession." The appellate court below though affirmed the judgment and order of the trial court took the view that the questions of adverse possession does not arise in this case and concluded that Sailendra continued to be a tenant by holding over. 

 15. The trial court fell into an error in its finding There is no adverse possession where the relationship is that of landlord and tenant (See Sk. Abdul Latif Vs. Malek 38 DLR (AD) 22. Next, when a tenant continues to stay on the land after the termination of the lease, but does so on the terms of the lease and on payment of rent his possession cannot be adverse to the landlord See Raishaeb Pandit vs. Bombay, Baroda Rly. 39 CWN 552 PC. The nearest approach was made by the appellate court below when it observed that the suit land belonged to the municipality and the defendants through Sailendra "occupied the suit land as tenants under the Municipality." Once this finding is established the rest becomes easier but regrettably the appellate court also fell into error by holding that after the acquisition of the rent receiving interest -Municipality ceased to have any right to the suit bad." This fallacious reasoning took place for the simple reason that the basic facts were ignored namely; (a) The plaintiff leased to defendant (b) defendant paid rent to the plaintiff as landlord. Therefore the defendant is estopped denying the title of the plaintiff. Section 116 Evidence Act. Section 2A provides that the Government may, in public interest, exempt by general or special order the interests of any local authority in any land or class of lands from acquisition under the provisions of the Act. The Municipality had leased this property to the defendant as far back as in 1921. Thereafter the Bengal Municipal Act 1932 was promulgated. It has been noticed already that the Municipality as a juristic person could hold and dispose of the property. In 1956 when the rent receiving interests were acquired the question is whether the interests of the Municipality which at one point of time belonged to a rent receiver stood acquired. Mr. Pal argued that the onus is upon the Municipality to prove that this interest had been exempted from the operation of law. This argument does not appeal to reason when considered in the light of section 85 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act which expressly excluded the property of the local authority from its operation. 

 17. What has been overlooked in the contention is that this property had already vested in the Municipality and the Municipality is not a rent receiver. Section 2A is an enabling power and has been enacted as a precaution which therefore reinforces the view that such interests are exempt from acquisition, Moreover, section 3 of the S.A.T. Act contemplates a notification when the Government decides to acquire the interest of the rent receivers including their interests which for the time being are under management of the Court of wards but no such notification is in existence and therefore the onus will be upon the party which alleged the existence of such notification. If the onus is not discharged, the position will be that no such notification had been issued. Therefore, the further probing into the matter becomes irrelevant. Hence the position remains between the parties as landlord and tenant. And there ends the matter.
